name: The Law of Triviality
statement: The time a group spends on an issue is inversely proportional to how much it matters.
statementAccent: inversely proportional to how much it matters
meaning: The law of triviality holds that an organisation, especially a committee, devotes attention to an issue in inverse proportion to its actual importance or cost. Groups give disproportionate weight to trivial, easily grasped matters while under-scrutinising the important, complex, or expensive ones. In software culture the same pattern is called bikeshedding, from Parkinson's image of a committee waving through a nuclear reactor but bickering endlessly over a bicycle shed. A bike-shed discussion is one that consumes energy out of all proportion to its stakes.
mechanism: The driving force is comprehensibility and the sense of competence it confers. A vast, technical, expensive item, a nuclear reactor, is beyond most committee members, so rather than engage they defer, assuming someone else checked the details. A trivial item, a bicycle shed or the coffee budget, is within everyone's grasp, so everyone feels qualified to weigh in and does. Because contributing an opinion is how members demonstrate diligence and belonging, the easy items lower the barrier to participation and attract a flood of it, while the consequential ones pass in near silence.

examples.text: Parkinson's finance committee approves a ten-million-pound atomic reactor in about two and a half minutes, then argues for three-quarters of an hour over a three-hundred-and-fifty-pound bicycle shed, and longer still over the annual coffee bill.

examples.tag: The colour of the bike shed
examples.text: In Poul-Henning Kamp's FreeBSD example, a deep change in technical infrastructure passes with little comment while a cosmetic detail, the proverbial colour of the bike shed, draws a storm of replies.
A board may nod through an opaque capital budget quickly and then spend most of the meeting debating the office renovation, the logo, or the catering, items every member can picture and judge.

variants.name: Bikeshedding
variants.text: The software-culture name, popularised by Poul-Henning Kamp on a FreeBSD mailing list in 1999, for disproportionate argument over trivia; 'what colour should the bike shed be?' became the shorthand.

variants.name: Not the same as Parkinson's Law
variants.text: It comes from the same book as the more famous Parkinson's Law, that work expands to fill the time available, but is a separate idea and should not be conflated with it.

whyItMatters: It explains how agendas get distorted so that low-stakes, high-comprehension items crowd out the high-stakes, high-complexity ones, degrading consequential decisions. Boards and committees can appear to exercise vigorous oversight of trivia while effectively rubber-stamping the choices that carry the real risk, precisely because those are hard to scrutinise. In engineering teams, naming the pattern as bikeshedding is itself a defence, letting maintainers recognise and shut down debate that has grown out of proportion to what is at stake.

working.text: notice when discussion time is running inversely to importance, a sign the easy items are crowding out the vital ones.
ensure complex, costly choices get genuine scrutiny rather than deference, since their difficulty is what lets them slip through.
call out bikeshedding when a cosmetic detail attracts disproportionate argument, to reclaim attention for what matters.

limits: It is an illustrative heuristic, not a measured relationship: Parkinson wrote as a satirist, and the committee scene and its figures are a fictional illustration rather than data, so the 'inverse proportion' phrasing is rhetorical. Nor is disproportionate attention always irrational; small recurring costs, precedent-setting items, and morale can genuinely warrant discussion, and quick approval of a large item may reflect legitimate prior vetting rather than negligence. The effect is strongest where members lack expertise on the big item and feel accountable to be seen participating, and weaker where real expertise or clear ownership exists.
misreadings: It is not the same as Parkinson's Law proper, that work expands to fill the time available; the two are distinct ideas from the same book. Bikeshedding is not old slang but a term traceable to Kamp's 1999 email, decades after Parkinson. The reactor, shed, and coffee figures are Parkinson's invented example, not a report of a real meeting. And the claim is about disproportionate attention, not that small matters are worthless.
origin: Set out by C. Northcote Parkinson in his 1957 book 'Parkinson's Law, or the Pursuit of Progress', in the chapter 'High Finance, or the Point of Vanishing Interest'; the software term 'bikeshedding' was popularised by Poul-Henning Kamp on a FreeBSD mailing list in 1999.

sources.text: Law of triviality, Wikipedia. — Parkinson's committee example, the figures, and Kamp's bikeshedding coinage.
Kamp, 'A bike shed (any colour will do on greener grass...)', FreeBSD mailing list, 2 October 1999 (archived). — the origin of the bike-shed metaphor in software culture.
